summary: Defines the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option for IPCP. It lets two peers on a PPP link say they support Mobile IP, so foreign agents need not give each mobile node a unique address.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IP lets a device keep the same IP address while it moves between networks. RFC 2290 fixes the part that was missing for PPP links: a new option in the PPP address negotiation that lets the device and its peer say plainly whether Mobile IP is supported, and which kind of temporary address the device should use.

questions: what is the mobile-ipv4 ipcp option
how does mobile ip work over ppp
how does a mobile node share a foreign agent care-of address
subtitle: An IPCP option that lets a mobile node and its PPP peer agree on how Mobile IP should work on the link.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP was written to work over any link, but its interaction with PPP was left underspecified, and the result was that Mobile IP was applied in the wrong way whenever a mobile node connected over PPP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Mobile-IPv4 option to the Internet Protocol Control Protocol, carrying the mobile node's home address, so that the two ends of the link can agree on whether the node is at home, should use an address of its own, or should share the peer's address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2290 is a Proposed Standard from February 1998. It updates RFC 2002 and has been updated by RFC 2794.

today: RFC 2290 is a Proposed Standard from February 1998. It updates RFC 2002 and has itself been updated by RFC 2794.

sections.title: Overview and Requirements
sections.content:
Mobile IP, defined in RFC 2002, routes packets to a mobile node wherever it is attached to the Internet, without changing its IP address. It is designed to run over any media and any data link layer, but the RFC points out that its interaction with PPP was underspecified, and that the result was an inappropriate application of Mobile IP whenever mobile nodes connected over PPP.

The fix is a new option for the Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP), the part of PPP that negotiates IP addresses. The mobile node and its peer use the Mobile-IPv4 option to negotiate the right way to use Mobile IP over the link. The option is designed to work together with the existing IP-Address option, not to replace it.

Four requirements shape the design. The option must stay backwards compatible with conventional nodes that know nothing about Mobile IP. It must cover the variety of scenarios shown in the examples. It must not duplicate what the IP-Address option already does. And a unique address must not be given to a mobile node unless it is truly needed: no address is assigned to a node that connects to its home link, nor to a node that connects to a foreign agent and uses that agent's care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP had no defined way to work over PPP, so mobile nodes ended up using it wrongly. This RFC adds one option to the PPP address negotiation and states four rules the design must follow, including that a mobile node should not be given an address of its own unless it really needs one.

sections.title: Mobile IP Roles and Care-of Addresses
sections.content:
Three roles matter for this option. A mobile node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment from one link to another, and that can keep communicating with its permanent home address from its current location. A home agent is a router with an interface on the mobile node's home link; it intercepts packets bound for the mobile node's home address and tunnels them to the node's care-of address when the node is on a foreign link. A foreign agent is a router with an interface on the link the mobile node is visiting; it removes the tunnel headers and delivers the packets, and may also act as the default router. The peer is the other end of the PPP link, and it may support home agent functionality, foreign agent functionality, both, or neither.

There are two kinds of care-of address. A co-located care-of address is a temporary address assigned to the mobile node itself, which then becomes the exit point of the tunnel and removes the tunnel headers itself. Only one mobile node can hold such an address at a time. A foreign agent care-of address belongs to a foreign agent on the visited link, which does the decapsulation and delivery, and many mobile nodes can share the same one.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node keeps its home address wherever it goes. A home agent on the home network forwards packets to it, and a foreign agent on the visited network can deliver them. A care-of address is the address the node is reached at, and it either belongs to the node alone or is shared with other mobile nodes.

sections.title: Why the Negotiation Went Wrong
sections.content:
Mobile IP defines two ways to reach a node away from home, and the RFC walks through the IPCP exchange to show that only one of them could ever be used over PPP.

The mobile node connects to a peer and proposes its home address in a Configure-Request carrying the IP-Address option. The peer cannot tell whether this came from a mobile node offering its home address or from a conventional node offering an address that is not routable, so it must conservatively answer with a Configure-Nak that supplies a topologically appropriate address. The mobile node then cannot tell whether that rejection came from a foreign agent being careful or from a peer that has no Mobile IP at all, so it must conservatively assume the peer does not implement Mobile IP and accept the assigned address as a co-located care-of address.

That defeats the point of a foreign agent care-of address, which is meant to be shared by many mobile nodes so that each one does not need a unique address. Even if the peer is a foreign agent and sends an Agent Advertisement once IPCP reaches the Opened state, the node has already negotiated a routable address and is likely using it as a co-located care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: Neither side of the PPP link could tell what the other meant, so both played safe. The mobile node ended up with an address of its own even when its peer was a foreign agent that could have shared one address with many mobile nodes.

sections.title: The Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option
sections.content:
The option is a short field carried inside the PPP configuration messages. It has a Type of 4, a Length of 6 bytes for the whole option, and a Mobile Node's Home Address field holding a 32-bit address. The address field carries the home address of the mobile node sending the option in a Configure-Request, and the unmodified home address of the mobile node when the option is sent in a Configure-Ack or a Configure-Reject. The field must not be zero.

Nakking this option is undefined, and implementations complying with this version of the specification must not send a Configure-Nak carrying it. The default value of the option is the sending mobile node's home address.

The RFC uses short names in the rest of the document. Request stands for Configure-Request, Reject for Configure-Reject, Ack for Configure-Ack and Nak for Configure-Nak. MIPv4 stands for the Mobile-IPv4 option and IP for the IP-Address option. In the notation, home is a mobile node's home address, coa is a care-of address, and 0 is the all-zeroes address, which is the way a node asks to be given one.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is six bytes long: a type number, a length, and the mobile node's home address. It never asks to be rejected with a Configure-Nak, and if it is left out, the mobile node's home address is assumed.

sections.title: The Negotiation Rules
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven numbered requests that a node may send, each with the legal replies from the peer, an interpretation of each reply and a suggested next step. A node that is not acting as a mobile node must not include the Mobile-IPv4 option in any Configure-Request, and it must never send a Configure-Nak containing it. A peer that acts as neither home agent nor foreign agent should reject any request that contains the option. A peer that accepts it should send an Agent Advertisement immediately once IPCP for that link reaches the Opened state.

A mobile node should begin with the request in item 1, which asks for the co-located care-of address it prefers, or the request in item 4, which asks to run Mobile IP without an address of its own. The peer answers with a Configure-Nak giving a co-located care-of address, a Configure-Nak saying that the node is at home and needs no care-of address, or a Configure-Reject saying that no co-located address can be assigned but the peer can act as a foreign agent.

If the peer rejects the option because it does not implement it, the mobile node falls back to the IP-Address option, starting with the home address when it is on its home link and with the all-zeroes address otherwise. A mobile node that receives a Configure-Ack containing the Mobile-IPv4 option must receive an Agent Advertisement before it sends a Registration Request when it is on a foreign link, because the peer may be a foreign agent whose policy requires registration even when the node uses a co-located address.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives a table of what the mobile node may ask for and what the peer may answer, and what each answer means. The peer can supply an address, say the node is at home, or refuse the option and act as a foreign agent instead.

sections.title: Example Scenarios
sections.content:
Six worked examples show the option in use, with the request and the response on the same line and numbered to match the rules above.

In the first scenario, the mobile node asks for a co-located care-of address and the peer, a foreign agent that can supply one, answers with a Nak giving the address. The node then requests that address and gets an Ack. The node waits for an Agent Advertisement, and if the advertisement has the R bit set, the node registers using the co-located address via the foreign agent; otherwise it registers directly with its home agent.

In the second scenario, the foreign agent has no pool of addresses to give, so it rejects the address request but accepts the option, and the node registers using the peer's foreign agent care-of address. In the third, the peer decides the node is at home and tells it so, and the node de-registers with its home agent. The remaining scenarios cover a peer that wants the node to use a foreign agent address, and two cases where the peer does not implement the option at all, with and without the ability to assign dynamic addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Six examples show what happens in practice: the peer supplies an address, cannot supply one, decides the node is at home, or does not understand the option. In each case the RFC states which registration the mobile node then makes.

sections.title: Other Options and Move Detection
sections.content:
A mobile node must not include the deprecated IP-Addresses option in any Configure-Request that also carries the Mobile-IPv4 option or the IP-Address option. It may include an IP-Compression-Protocol option and other options that do not negotiate IP addresses. If the two ends agree in IPCP to use Van Jacobson header compression, the mobile node must not set the 'V' bit in its Mobile IP Registration Request, since the link already compresses the headers and asking again causes confusion.

Because moving usually changes the mobile node's PPP peer, the node must be ready to renegotiate IPCP at any time, including both options described in this RFC, and it must renegotiate when it receives a Configure-Request from its peer. Some wireless links hand off without tearing the PPP link down, so the node must also run its move detection algorithms and register whenever it detects a change in connectivity. A node that does not hear from its current foreign agent within the lifetime that agent advertised must assume it has lost contact, and should register with a new foreign agent straight away if one has advertised itself. A node that detects movement by comparing network prefixes must register when an advertisement arrives from an agent on a different prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving changes the PPP peer, so the node has to be ready to renegotiate the link at any time. It must also notice when it has arrived somewhere else, even if the PPP link itself never dropped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the document introduces no known security threats beyond those that face any node on the Internet that connects over PPP, implements Mobile IP, or both.

It then names the protections that apply. Service providers should use cryptographically strong authentication, such as CHAP, to prevent theft of service. Users who need confidentiality should use PPP link encryption, IP-layer encryption or application-layer encryption, depending on their requirements. Mobile IP authentication protects against the trivial denial-of-service attacks that could otherwise be made against a mobile node and its home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no new threats of its own. It points to the existing protections: strong PPP authentication, encryption where confidentiality is needed, and the Mobile IP authentication that guards the node and its home agent.
